Symptoms: Impetigo is a bacterial infection characterized by erythematous macules that rapidly evolve into vesicles or pustules. Non-bullous impetigo is characterized by small erythematous macules that rapidly evolve into vesicles or pustules. Bullous impetigo is characterized by larger (0.5–2-cm), flaccid, fluid-filled bullae on an erythematous base or normal-appearing skin. Systemic symptoms are uncommon in uncomplicated impetigo but may signal a deeper infected infection such as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), which is associated with nephritogenic strains of *S pyogenes*
Causes: Impetigo is a toxin-mediated bacterial virulence-mediated disease characterized primarily by bacterial virulence factors. The etiology of impetigo is directly linked to specific bacterial virulence factors. *S. aureus* or *S. pyogenes* produce exfoliative toxins (exfoliatins A and B), which are highly specific serine proteases that act as "molecular scissors" . Risk Factories for impetigo include pre-existing skin conditions like atopic dermatitis, warm/humid climates, pre-existing immunosuppression or diabetes mellitus, and community-associated methicillin-residue-resistant *S. aureus*
Treatment: Medications: Topical antimicrobials. Oral antimicrobials. Adjunctive measures. Decolonization strategies.
When to See a Doctor: See a dermatologist if skin lesions spread rapidly or involve more than five to ten sites. See a dermatologist if lesions show no improvement after 48 to 72 hours of topical antibiotic use. See a dermatologist if lesions persist for more than three to five years.
